certHelp.title: Install the distribution agent on a site host
certHelp.intro: Install an agent on each host where certificates should auto-rotate. The agent periodically checks jt-ipam for a newer version and, if found, downloads it, writes it to the right paths, runs a config-test, reloads the service, and rolls back on failure.
certHelp.step1: Create an agent in the Distribution Agents tab and copy its one-time key.
certHelp.step2: After creating the agent, open it (the dialog shown right after, or the View action in the list) to get its ready-to-paste one-line install command — key filled in, root/sudo auto-detected. Run it on the target host as root.
certHelp.step3: After pasting the config, run --dry-run on the host to verify; the timer then distributes automatically (advanced: you can also edit the config's DEPLOY_1_* by hand).
certHelp.step3_hint: See "Config help" for the config format and per-profile paths.
certHelp.step3_gen_a: Fastest: in the Distribution Agents list, click the
certHelp.step3_gen_b: tool in that agent's action column, pick certs + services, then paste the result back.
certHelp.distros: Supports Debian 11/12/13, Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04, RHEL/Rocky/AlmaLinux/CentOS, Fedora, openSUSE/SLES (auto-detects apt/dnf/yum/zypper). Keep JT_IPAM_INSECURE=1 if the server uses a self-signed cert.
certHelp.distros_note: Auto-detects apt / dnf / yum / zypper; keep JT_IPAM_INSECURE=1 if the server cert is self-signed.
certHelp.after_install_gen: Once the agent is installed, come back to this list and click the "Generate config" tool in its action column to quickly build its deployment config (which certificates to push, which service profile to use).
certHelp.service_note: Installed units (systemd): jt-ipam-cert-agent.timer (schedule, daily) + jt-ipam-cert-agent.service (each run). Full logs: journalctl -u jt-ipam-cert-agent.service (add -f to follow). Run once now: systemctl start jt-ipam-cert-agent.service.
certHelp.profiles: Built-in profiles: nginx / apache(httpd) / haproxy / postfix / dovecot / pve / pmg / pbs / zimbra / generic (generic requires custom *_path and reload).
certHelp.uninstall_note: Stops and removes the timer / service, the agent program, config and state; certificate files already deployed to your services are left untouched.
certHelp.requirements: Requirements: the agent is pure bash, depending only on curl + coreutils (no Python / jq / YAML); run as root (or an account with permission to write the cert paths and run the reload commands); the installer sets up a systemd timer (daily by default).
certHelp.autoupdate: Self-update: when a newer agent is available on the server, the agent downloads it, verifies the sha256, atomically replaces itself and re-execs (a failure is logged and never affects that run's deployment). Set AUTO_UPDATE=false in config to disable. The Distribution Agents list shows each agent's current version and flags "update available" when it lags.

scanAgentHelp.title: Scan agent install guide
scanAgentHelp.intro: A scan agent runs on a Linux host inside the target segment and connects OUT to jt-ipam. It periodically pulls the subnets to scan, runs ping/ARP, and pushes results back with its key. The server never needs inbound access to the agent.
scanAgentHelp.step1: Click Create here to make an agent — you get a one-time enrollment key.
scanAgentHelp.step2: On a Linux host in the target segment, run the one-liner below (downloads the agent, sets up systemd, starts reporting).
scanAgentHelp.step3: In Subnets, set the subnets you want scanned to use this agent and enable scanning.
scanAgentHelp.oneliner_label: One-line install (run as root on the agent host)
scanAgentHelp.note: The key is shown only once (at create / rotate). The command includes JT_IPAM_INSECURE=1 for self-signed server certs.
scanAgentHelp.key_title: Agent created — copy the key now
scanAgentHelp.key_warn: The enrollment key for "{name}" is shown only once.
scanAgentHelp.key_note: Paste the one-liner on the agent host; then assign subnets to scan.
scanAgentHelp.install_paths: Installs to: program /opt/jt-ipam-agent/jt_ipam_agent.py, config /etc/jt-ipam-agent.env, service jt-ipam-scan-agent (systemctl status/restart jt-ipam-scan-agent; logs journalctl -u jt-ipam-scan-agent). Uses system python3, no extra packages.
scanAgentHelp.path_python: Uses the system python3 — no extra packages. After a key reset, just re-run the installer (it auto-restarts).
scanAgentHelp.assign_subnets_ph: Pick subnets this agent scans (same setting as the subnet edit page)

dns_admin.title: DNS Servers
dns_admin.help_powerdns: Enter the PowerDNS Authoritative HTTP API URL and X-API-Key (webserver/api must be enabled).
dns_admin.help_bind9: Operate BIND 9 via rndc / TSIG; TSIG key format algorithm:keyname:base64key.
dns_admin.help_unbound_opnsense: Uses the OPNsense Unbound REST API: create an API key/secret in OPNsense with Unbound access.
dns_admin.help_windows_dns: Connects to the Windows DNS host over WinRM; the account needs DNS admin rights. Windows Server opens only HTTP 5985 by default (content is NTLM-encrypted); with a certificate listener you can use HTTPS 5986, turning off "Verify TLS certificate" for a self-signed certificate.
dns_admin.help_ucs: Calls the Univention UCS UDM REST API (/univention/udm/…) directly — not the internal BIND9. API URL = https://<ucs-host>; use an account with DNS write rights (e.g. Administrator); turn off TLS verification for self-signed certs.
dns_admin.error_username_required: Username is required (this DNS type uses credential auth)
dns_admin.zones_hint: DNS has no way to enumerate zones, so the zones to sync must be listed explicitly (including reverse zones). Without them the sync completes but returns nothing. BIND must also allow this system to AXFR those zones (allow-transfer).
dns_admin.help_technitium: Enter the Technitium console URL (by default http://host:5380 or https://host:53443) and an API token. View permission is enough: create a dedicated user and group, give it view permission for Zones, and give the group view permission on each zone to sync. Technitium does not list zones the account cannot read (they look like they do not exist), and new zones only grant the administrator groups by default, so remember to add zones created later. Set up DHCP separately under "Technitium DHCP".
dns_admin.technitium_test_ok: Connected: Technitium {version}, account {user}, {n} zones readable. Technitium does not list zones the account cannot read: if the count is lower than expected, check the account's view permission on each zone.
dns_admin.technitium_unreadable: {n} zones cannot be read: {zones}. Give the account's group view permission on those zones in Technitium, otherwise their records are not synced.
dns_admin.technitium_can_modify: This token can modify zones. jt-ipam only reads; an account with view permission only is recommended.
dns_admin.verify_tls_winrm_hint: Turn off when WinRM HTTPS uses a self-signed certificate; traffic stays HTTPS-encrypted, only the certificate is not checked (a certificate from an internal CA is better).
dns_admin.winrm_transport_hint: HTTP 5985 by default, because the Windows Server firewall blocks HTTPS 5986 by default (HTTPS needs a certificate listener and a firewall rule). Over HTTP the content and credentials are always NTLM-encrypted, never sent in clear. Leave the port empty for the default.
dns_admin.compare_group_hint: Put DNS servers whose content should match (for example primary/secondary or AD-integrated) in one comparison group: identical records are shown once, and the servers' data is compared after each pull. jt-ipam does not sync records between the servers.
dns_admin.cg_intro: Put DNS servers whose content should match (primary/secondary, AD-integrated, multi-primary and so on, replicating among themselves) in one group. jt-ipam does not sync or change records between them; it only compares the data pulled from each one. The DNS records page, anomaly detection and IP change assessment show identical records once with the servers that hold them; after each pull the group is compared, differences are listed, and confirmed ones are alerted through notifications. A, AAAA and PTR records are compared; AD service locator data (_msdcs, TrustAnchors, DomainDnsZones, ForestDnsZones) is not; when only some zones are replicated, the others can be left out.
dns_admin.cg_members_ph: Choose DNS servers whose content should match
dns_admin.cg_members_hint: At least two are needed for a comparison; a server already in another group moves here; disabled servers are left out. Different products can be mixed (for example Windows DNS and UCS), but Unbound (OPNsense) holds host overrides rather than full zones, so it can only be grouped with other Unbound servers.
dns_admin.cg_grace_hint: Replication between the servers takes time: a difference is confirmed, and alerted, only when the server missing it is pulled again at least this long after the difference appeared and still lacks it.
dns_admin.cg_excluded_ph: Pick or type zones (empty = compare all)
dns_admin.cg_excluded_hint: When the servers replicate only some zones, or one of them also holds zones of its own, list those zones here: a zone on only one server is not a difference and its records are not compared. The group is compared again when you save.
dns_admin.cg_exclude_zone_confirm: Stop comparing zone "{zone}"? You can undo it under "Zones not compared" in the group settings.
dns_admin.cg_notify_hint: Notify administrators when a mismatch is confirmed and again when it is resolved (per "DNS comparison group mismatch" in notification settings).
dns_admin.cg_status_hint_ok: Every server in the group has the same records.
dns_admin.cg_status_hint_mismatch: Some differences are confirmed: the server missing them was pulled again after the grace period and still lacks them.
dns_admin.cg_status_hint_pending: There are differences, not confirmed yet: still within the grace period, or the server missing them has not been pulled again.
dns_admin.cg_status_hint_incomplete: A member's last pull failed or it has never been pulled, so no verdict yet.
dns_admin.cg_status_hint_single: Fewer than two enabled members, so there is nothing to compare.
dns_admin.cg_status_hint_never: Members are compared after each pull; you can also click Check now.
dns_admin.cg_status_hint_incompatible: Unbound (OPNsense) can only be grouped with other Unbound servers; move the other servers to another group.
dns_admin.cg_check_hint: The comparison uses the records jt-ipam has already pulled; for the latest data, click Pull on each server first. A difference is confirmed when the server missing it is pulled again {n} minutes or more after it appeared and still lacks it.
dns_admin.cg_delete_confirm: Delete this comparison group? Its servers return to no group and records are no longer merged (records on the servers are not affected).

librenms_admin.arp_create_require_fdb_hint: Only create when a switch MAC table (FDB) has also seen the MAC within 24 hours. Some devices keep ARP entries for hours or days (Cisco defaults to 4 hours; some keep them until the interface goes down or the device reboots), so ARP alone also creates addresses of devices that left long ago. MAC tables usually age out within minutes, so a recent sighting shows the device really sent traffic. Needs FDB sync on (MikroTik MAC tables count too).
librenms_admin.arp_create_no_fdb_warn: ARP only: after a device leaves, its address is still created for as long as the router keeps the ARP entry. Only turn this off where no switch MAC table is available and you know how long ARP entries live.
librenms_admin.arp_create_skip_dhcp_hint: Addresses inside a known DHCP pool are not created (they are handed to other devices later). Ranges come from the DHCP-related integrations.

anomaly.title: Anomaly Detection
anomaly.help: Run every detection rule: IP conflicts, MAC drift, stale addresses, unauthorised addresses, rogue DHCP servers, external exposure, stale DNS records, duplicate address records and suspicious changes.
anomaly.explain_ip_conflicts: One IP in the same network used by two or more machines. Two kinds of evidence: "ARP" means ARP observations (LibreNMS, scan agents, firewall ARP tables) saw two or more MACs in the last hour; "MAC keeps flipping" means the IP's MAC switched between the same two addresses 3 or more times in the last 24 hours (a scan agent sees only one MAC per sweep, so this catches conflicts when scans are far apart). Overlapping subnets are judged separately and never conflict with each other. Addresses tagged as locally administered have no vendor registration — virtual machines, containers and phone MAC randomisation all produce them. An IP showing both a real MAC and a randomised one is usually a single device that changed address (reconnect, migration, NIC failover) rather than two machines fighting over an IP. The ones worth acting on are those where both MACs resolve to a vendor and belong to different devices. Confidence is high when at least two machines are each seen by two or more sources, and low when the other side is reported by a single source (often a device's stale ARP cache). Hover "N sources" next to a MAC to see which devices and interfaces reported it. MACs marked "Likely misread" or "Likely stale cache" are listed but not counted as machines; when every MAC belongs to one host the row moves to "One host on several NICs (ARP flux)".
anomaly.explain_mac_drifts: A MAC moved to a different port on the same switch (seen on the new port in the last 24 hours, on another port within the previous 7 days): usually a device re-plugged or relocated. Appearing on different switches is the normal forwarding path and does not count. VM migrations, random-MAC roaming and moves between shared ports (uplinks, access points) are listed below for reference and are not notified.
anomaly.explain_ghost_ips: IPs marked as assigned in IPAM but with no sign of life for a long time (neither the scan agent nor LibreNMS has seen them). Usually decommissioned hosts whose records were never reclaimed — useful for cleaning up address space.
anomaly.explain_unauthorized_ips: IPs actually seen on the network but not recorded in IPAM. Could be a device configured without going through a request, or simply a record not added yet.
anomaly.rogue_dhcp_warn: These hosts answered a DHCP request on the segment but are not marked as DHCP servers. Usually that means something is plugged in that should not be — a consumer router, or a VM with DHCP left on — handing out wrong addresses and gateways to other machines. If one is legitimate, mark it as a DHCP server on that address's detail page.
anomaly.explain_rogue_dhcp: Hosts that answered DHCP on a segment but are not marked as DHCP servers. Something is handing out addresses that is not in your plan — usually a consumer router someone plugged in, or a VM with DHCP left on. Requires the "DHCP server discovery" probe to be enabled on the scan agent.
anomaly.scope_hint: Only the subnets listed here are checked. Guest, lab and contractor segments are noisy by nature, and leaving them in buries the findings that matter. This is the same setting as "Include in anomaly detection" on the subnet edit page.
anomaly.exp_dns_to_offline: DNS points at an offline host
anomaly.exp_hint: All of this comes from data already synced into jt-ipam (NAT rules, firewall rules, DNS records). Detection never contacts a firewall or any device.
anomaly.chg_bulk_delete: Bulk deletion in a short window
anomaly.explain_dangling_dns: DNS records pointing at an address that no longer exists in the IPAM, or that no source has seen in a long time. Besides sending people to a service that isn't there, someone else may claim that address and take over the name.
anomaly.explain_external_exposure: Addresses opened to the internet by NAT or a firewall rule whose state does not match — no monitoring at all, offline, or in an archived subnet. An open door nobody watches is the one to deal with first.
anomaly.explain_duplicate_ip_records: The same address has a record in each of two subnets that contain one another. Integration syncs stamp only one of them, so the other's liveness and hostname stay frozen at their old values.
anomaly.explain_suspicious_changes: A burst of changes in a short window, or changes from a source you would not expect. These are observed patterns only; whether they are a problem is your call.
anomaly.explain_fw_rule_rot: Parts of the active ruleset that are already wrong: port forwards whose target is not in IPAM (likely reclaimed), any-to-any permits (every protocol and port allowed, so that interface effectively has no firewall), and management ports (SSH/RDP/VNC/IPMI) open to any source on a WAN interface. Manual NAT entries, disabled rules, rules the firewall generates itself (such as Anti-Lockout), and rules limited to one protocol or port (such as allowing only ping) are excluded.
anomaly.explain_arp_only_liveness: These addresses look online, but the only evidence is an ARP record — and ARP carries no timestamp while the reporting device's cache never expires. A machine that was powered off weeks ago still reads as online here. To find out the real state, probe them with a scan agent or bring them under LibreNMS/Zabbix monitoring.
anomaly.explain_stale_device_links: These IPs are linked to a device but the address has changed MAC since that link was made — usually the address was handed to a different machine (common with DHCP), so the link now points at the wrong device. Nothing is unlinked automatically: whether to detach is a judgement call. Compare the current MAC against that device before changing or clearing it.
anomaly.sched_hint: A scheduled run only notifies about findings that are new since the last run. Detection reports the current state, not a stream of events; repeating an unresolved one every run is how a whole notification category gets muted.
anomaly.sched_enabled_hint: Off by default. The background scheduler (which wakes about every 5 minutes) runs it when due; results appear on this page.
anomaly.sched_interval_hint: Minimum 5 minutes — the background scheduler itself only wakes every 5 minutes, so anything shorter is not actually more responsive.
anomaly.sched_times_hint: Wall-clock times rather than "every N hours": interval scheduling drifts with each run. For anything more frequent, use "Every N minutes".
anomaly.sched_month_day_hint: Set 31 and a 30-day month (or February) runs on its last day rather than skipping the month entirely.
anomaly.ignore_done: Added to the ignore list; this category will no longer report this IP
anomaly.ignore_hint: For addresses that legitimately behave this way — a device with MAC randomisation on (Windows 11 / macOS / iOS / Android) changes its MAC on every connection.
anomaly.explain_mac_flapping: The same IP has been seen with several different MACs during the window. Usual causes: a DHCP pool being recycled, somebody manually taking a static address, or the device using MAC randomisation (the privacy feature in Windows 11 / macOS / iOS / Android, which picks a new locally administered address on every connection). A "yes" in the randomised column usually means the latter -- but it can also be someone spoofing a MAC, so this only states the facts and leaves the judgement to you. If it is expected, "Ignore this IP" stops it being reported.

anomaly.evidence_arp: ARP: several MACs within an hour
anomaly.filter_ph: Filter: IP / hostname / MAC / details… (applies to every tab)
anomaly.drift_reference_hint: These moved ports too, but are usually routine: a VM migrating between hosts, a phone's random MAC roaming between access points, or a move between two ports shared by many devices (roaming between access points, an uplink switchover or STP reconvergence).
anomaly.explain_identity_changes: The scan agent’s periodic detection now identifies a different device type or OS family for this address (a printer that became a Windows host, a camera that became a Linux server). The address may have been taken by another machine, the device replaced, or something is impersonating it. Going from unknown to known does not count, and a judgement that flips back and forth is not listed. For machines that legitimately change (dual boot), use “Ignore this IP”.
anomaly.unauthorized_truncated: Showing the {shown} most recently seen of {total}. Numbers this large usually mean a whole subnet was never registered: check the subnets first, or consider turning on automatic IP creation in the integration.
anomaly.arp_flux: One host on several NICs (ARP flux)
anomaly.explain_arp_flux: One IP is answered by two or more NICs of the same host: not two machines fighting over it, but a host answering ARP on interfaces that do not own the address. The usual cause is Linux's default arp_ignore=0 plus two subnets sharing one layer 2 (see "Subnets sharing one layer 2"); the router log keeps printing "arp: ... moved from ... to ...". Fix it on the host with net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_ignore=1 and net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_announce=2, saved under /etc/sysctl.d/ so it survives a reboot. "NIC" tells which of the device's interfaces each MAC belongs to (its registered IP or port name).
anomaly.explain_l2_subnet_bleed: Two IP subnets are really one broadcast domain: an IP in one subnet was answered by a MAC in use in the other, or one VLAN on a switch learned MACs from both. The segments are not isolated (for example a link between two switches joins them), which is also what causes ARP flux. If it is by design (two subnets on one VLAN) you can ignore it; otherwise check the switches' VLAN setup and the physical links between the segments. A MAC registered in several subnets (router subinterfaces) or registered but not in use is not used as evidence.
anomaly.suspect_corrupt_hint: Reported by a single source, no vendor, and spliced from two other MACs of the same IP (or one byte away from a MAC several sources agree on): most likely an SNMP walk caught the device's ARP table mid-change. Listed, but not counted as a machine.
anomaly.suspect_stale_cache_hint: A locally administered MAC reported by one device's ARP table while several other sources see another MAC: most likely that device's ARP cache has not expired yet. Listed, but not counted as a machine.
anomaly.confidence_hint: High: at least two machines each seen by two or more sources (or MAC flipping is recorded). Low: the other side is reported by a single source, often a device's stale ARP cache.

migration.help: Pull from your existing phpIPAM MySQL. First run dry-run to preview, then commit. on_conflict=skip is safe to re-run repeatedly during parallel use (already-imported rows untouched).
migration.intro_combined: Pull from phpIPAM. Private key is used once and not stored. Use dry-run first.

system.graylog_page_intro: jt-ipam generates a live IP → hostname / FQDN lookup endpoint so Graylog can automatically enrich log events that only carry an IP. Enable the endpoint and grab the URL here, then wire it into Graylog using the guide below.

system.graylog_g_url_or_http: or plain HTTP (dedicated port 8088, trusted LAN only):

system.graylog_g_apply_intro: Pick just one of the two methods below — you don't need both: an Extractor is the simplest and best for a single Input with simple rules; a Pipeline is more flexible and can span multiple Streams / add conditions.
system.graylog_g_ex: Go to System → Inputs, pick your Input → “Manage extractors” → “Get started”, choose a message that has the field → add a “Lookup Table” extractor on the source field → pick the lookup table you created and store the result in a new field. Every incoming message then gets enriched automatically. Best for a single Input with simple rules.
system.graylog_g_pl_title: Apply the lookup with a Pipeline
system.graylog_g_pl: For multiple streams or conditional logic, use a Pipeline instead. Under System → Pipelines create a pipeline connected to the target Stream, and in a stage add a rule that calls lookup_value() to query the table and set_field() to write the result. The first argument of lookup_value is the Lookup Table name (not the path).
system.graylog_g_pl_fw: Under System → Pipelines add a rule that calls lookup_value() to fetch this DSV's value and set_field() to write a new field. The first argument of lookup_value is the Lookup Table name (not the path). Set the “log field” (configured in Step 2) to the parsed filterlog field: bind the rule DSV to rid, the alias DSV to your alias field.
system.graylog_g_field_label: Log field to look up (auto-filled into the example below):
system.graylog_g_lan: Looking up public IPs against this table is pointless (it only contains your internal IPs). In the pipeline rule, use cidr_match() to first test whether the IP falls within the RFC1918 private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) and only look it up when it does — saving resources and avoiding false hits. Replace src_ip with your actual IP field name:
system.graylog_g_note: Tip: the lookup_value() key must be cast with to_string(); the second argument of cidr_match() must be cast with to_ip(). If your messages carry both source and destination IPs, duplicate the rule for dst_ip → dst_hostname.

system.rdp_engine_hint: The default is guacd, handled by the jt-ipam-guacd service (see its status below). It is the most compatible — including xrdp and GNOME Remote Login on Linux — and needs no virtual display; while guacd is not running, connections use aardwolf or FreeRDP instead. aardwolf is the built-in pure-Python implementation and works against Windows targets, but xrdp and GNOME Remote Login reject its NTLM authentication. FreeRDP is also broadly compatible but requires FreeRDP and a virtual display on this host. The change applies to new connections.
system.rdp_engine_missing: This server does not yet have what the FreeRDP engine needs (missing {pkgs}). Install them and reload this page; until then, selecting FreeRDP will not connect.
system.rdp_engine_no_aardwolf: This server has no aardwolf (there is no prebuilt package for Python {python}). aardwolf is an optional fallback engine; with RDP set to aardwolf or VNC set to built-in, those consoles cannot connect — switch back to guacd (the default).
system.port_filter_pseudo_hint: When importing ports from integrations, skip and prune pseudo interfaces matching the name patterns below (Windows NDIS filters, WAN Miniport, tunnels, etc.). When off, nothing is filtered or pruned.
system.port_ignore_patterns_hint: One regular expression per line (matched against the interface name, case-insensitive). Leave empty to use the built-in defaults. Physical switch and Linux port names do not match these patterns and are unaffected.
system.vnc_engine_hint: The default is guacd, which handles the screen in the jt-ipam-guacd service and supports VNC servers that ask for a username; while guacd is not running, connections use the built-in engine (aardwolf) instead. The change applies to new connections.
system.ssh_engine_hint: The built-in engine is the xterm.js terminal in the browser. guacd draws the terminal on the server and the browser receives the screen, so URLs in it cannot be clicked (use the built-in engine if you need that); copy and paste with Ctrl+Shift+C / Ctrl+Shift+V (⌘C / ⌘V on a Mac). Host keys are still confirmed once and then pinned. The change applies to new connections.
system.guacd_protocol_missing: guacd has no support for {protocols}; those protocols will not connect while set to guacd.
system.guacd_hint: guacd is the server side of Apache Guacamole, prebuilt by jt-ipam and run locally only as the jt-ipam-guacd service. It is the default engine for RDP and VNC (installed automatically on install and upgrade); SSH can be switched to it separately.
system.sftp_max_mb_hint: Default 100 MB (meant for config files, certificates and logs); raise it to move larger files. Files travel over the console WebSocket in 256 KB pieces, through any reverse proxy in front and the IPAM nginx; changing the limit runs a real test of that path. Downloads over 64 MB are written straight to disk (Chrome, Edge; other browsers are limited to 2 GB).
system.sftp_probe_ok: Transfer path OK: upload about {up}/s, download about {down}/s. At this speed a {max} file takes about {upTime} to upload and {downTime} to download.
system.sftp_probe_ws_blocked: The WebSocket cannot reach the SFTP path (code {code}): the reverse proxy in front or the IPAM nginx does not enable WebSocket for /api/v1/addresses/…/sftp/ws. SFTP and the other consoles will not work.
system.sftp_probe_msg_too_big: Disconnected as "message too big" (code 1009) at {done} of {total}: a layer on the path, most likely the reverse proxy in front or a WAF, limits the size of a WebSocket message. SFTP downloads send 256 KB messages; allow at least 1 MB.
system.sftp_probe_closed: The connection was cut at {done} of {total} (code {code}): a layer on the path limits WebSocket volume or duration. Check the WebSocket settings of the reverse proxy in front and the IPAM nginx.
system.sftp_probe_no_data_up: Upload data does not get through: the server received nothing new for {sec} s ({done} of {total} received). A layer on the path swallows data sent back to back.
system.sftp_probe_no_data_down: Download data does not arrive: nothing new for {sec} s ({done} of {total} received).
system.sftp_probe_note: Measured from this browser, through every layer between you and the server. Users on other networks may take a different path.
system.sftp_max_mb_range: The SFTP limit must be between 1 and 102400 MB (100 GB)
system.graylog_token_hint2: The token is not loaded with this page: it is fetched when you click Show or copy a URL, and every fetch is audited. It expires (choose the validity when you regenerate it), and administrators are notified 14, 7 and 1 days before.

system.graylog_sources_hint: When set, lookups are accepted only from these addresses (over HTTPS and port 8088); usually the Graylog server. Empty means no restriction.

llm_settings.title: LLM / AI global settings
llm_settings.admin_note: This page holds {strong}; changes overwrite .env and persist to system_settings. All users and automation (embedding / chat / MCP) share this config.
llm_settings.num_ctx_hint: Max tokens the chat model can see at once. Blank or 0 = use the model/Ollama default (usually 4096). Tool-heavy chats with large injected data can exceed the default and get truncated (the model 'forgets' earlier content); raise it to e.g. 8192 / 16384 / 32768. Larger uses more RAM/VRAM. Affects chat only, not the embedding model.
llm_settings.chat_thinking: Let the model think before answering in AI chat
llm_settings.chat_thinking_hint: On (default): thinking models reason first and the chat shows "thinking". Off: every chat turn sends the controls that turn thinking off (Ollama's think:false; reasoning_effort and friends for OpenAI-compatible servers and gateways such as LiteLLM), which answers much faster — useful when the model thinks but you want quick replies. A control the server does not accept is dropped automatically. AI review and AI interpretation always turn thinking off, regardless of this setting.
llm_settings.mcp_ext_title: Expose MCP (let other systems call it)
llm_settings.mcp_ext_hint: When on, other systems (external LLM clients, automation) can call this site's MCP endpoint over HTTP to query data. Off by default — must be turned on to accept external calls.
llm_settings.mcp_transport_note: (in your client pick HTTP / Streamable, not SSE)
llm_settings.mcp_auth_choose: either one (header name on the left, value on the right):
llm_settings.mcp_key_rotate_confirm: Regenerating immediately invalidates the old key; connected systems must update. Continue?
llm_settings.mcp_key_hint: This key is read-only: external systems can only query — the 6 data-changing tools are always blocked. It is stored encrypted and authorized within the current admin's visibility; regenerate immediately if leaked. The key expires (choose the validity when you generate or replace it); administrators are notified 14, 7 and 1 days before.
llm_settings.mcp_gen_hint: Paste the snippet into the tool's config file to connect to this MCP. The API key is filled in for you; exact schema may vary by tool/version.
llm_settings.mcp_gen_inline_hint: One-click config for Claude Desktop / opencode / mcpo and more
llm_settings.embedding_url_hint: Only needed when the embedding model runs elsewhere; leave empty to use the URL above. Provider, API key and timeout are shared.
llm_settings.tools_intro: The AI assistant and external MCP clients can call these {n} tools ({m} of which change data and require confirmation). Read-only tools answer instantly; mutating ones pause in the AI chat for you to confirm.
llm_settings.interpret_scope: Used by: "AI triage" for unauthorized IPs, "Ask AI to read this" in IP investigation, and the AI reading of firewall rule changes. All three are on-demand features that hand a bundle of evidence to the model for a conclusion.
llm_settings.interpret_model_hint: Leave empty to use the same model as AI chat. Chat needs quick responses; interpretation reads all the evidence at once before concluding — you can point it at a model with better judgement. Each result shows the model that actually wrote it.
llm_settings.interpret_num_ctx_hint: Leave empty to use the chat model's setting (currently {n}). Raise it when there is a lot of evidence (a long change history, many target addresses) so the prompt is not truncated; the cost is more memory/VRAM.
llm_settings.audit_enabled_hint: When on, IPAM data is sent to the language model at the times set below to look for anything suspicious or a security concern. Off by default.
llm_settings.audit_warning: The review sends structural data about subnets, IPs and devices (addresses, hostnames, status, last-seen times) to the LLM server you configured. Sampling follows the permissions of the account it runs as and never exceeds what that account can see — but do make sure that LLM server is somewhere you trust.
llm_settings.audit_model_hint: Leave empty to use the same model as AI chat. A review sends a lot of data in one batch, which is a different trade-off from interactive chat — you can point it at a larger model for better judgement, or a smaller one to save compute.
llm_settings.audit_times_hint: Runs once at each of these times on scheduled days (which days is set by the frequency above), in the server's timezone ({tz}). Times rather than an interval, because an interval drifts with each run — after a few days nobody can say whether it hits the LLM at 3am or mid-morning.
llm_settings.audit_scope_hint: Only the subnets listed here are sent to the model. This is the same setting as "Include in AI review" on the subnet edit page — changing either changes both.
llm_settings.audit_num_ctx_hint: Leave empty to use the chat model's setting (currently {n}). This decides how many records fit in one batch: larger means fewer batches and a faster run, at the cost of memory/VRAM. Too small and the data is split into many batches, which also makes cross-subnet problems easier for the model to miss.
llm_settings.provider_hint: OpenAI-compatible covers ChatGPT, vLLM, LM Studio, OpenRouter and others; Ollama also exposes a /v1 compatibility layer.
llm_settings.provider_egress_warn: With an external service, your subnets, hostnames and topology are sent to that provider. Keep the self-hosted Ollama if data must not leave your network.
llm_settings.api_base_hint: Up to /v1 is enough (e.g. https://api.openai.com/v1); /v1 is appended if omitted.
llm_settings.api_key_hint: Local endpoints (vLLM, LM Studio) usually need no key; leave blank. The key is stored for calls only and never returned to the browser.
llm_settings.embed_ok: Dimensions match ({dim}); semantic search is usable.
llm_settings.embed_dim_mismatch: The model returns {dim} dimensions but the database column holds {expected} — they do not match, so nothing will ever be indexed. Choose an embedding model of the matching size.
llm_settings.embed_hint: The embedding model must output {expected} dimensions (the database column size). A mismatch raises no visible error — the only symptom is that semantic search never returns anything — so check after changing the model.
llm_settings.reindex_hint: After changing the embedding model, existing records still hold the old vectors (or none); rebuild once so semantic search covers them. This can take several minutes depending on how much data you have.
llm_settings.audit_month_day_hint: If you pick the 31st, months with 30 days (and February) run on their last day instead, rather than skipping the month entirely.
llm_settings.think_off: {who}: thinking is off as requested, answered in {sec} s
llm_settings.think_why_empty: the answer is empty; the gateway may be hiding the reasoning
llm_settings.think_on_hint: When the model ignores this, AI audit, AI interpretation (and AI chat with thinking off) get slow, and the reasoning can use up the answer's token budget. Use Ollama 0.9 or later; through LiteLLM, prefix the model with ollama/ or ollama_chat/; for llama.cpp, upgrade to b10434 or later or start it with --reasoning-budget 0.

system_settings.title: System Settings (global)
system_settings.liveness_sources_hint: Only the selected sources decide whether an address is online. The LibreNMS ARP API returns no timestamp and a DHCP lease may be days old, so a powered-off machine keeps looking online; a firewall's own ARP table and VPN sessions do time out, so they are trusted by default.
system_settings.cooldown_days_hint: After an address is released (deleted) it is not offered for reallocation during this window, and creating it by hand is refused. Things outside IPAM still point at it: DNS records and caches, firewall rules, ACLs, certificate SANs, monitoring. Handing it to another machine too early produces the hardest kind of fault to diagnose. Default 30 days; 0 disables it. An admin can clear an individual address early, which is recorded.
system_settings.rack_embed_hint: Once enabled, racks you have individually shared are available at a URL (carrying a token) that other systems can embed as an image, such as a LibreNMS dashboard. Each rack must also be turned on from the Racks page.
system_settings.rack_embed_token_hint: This is a key: anyone holding it can see the diagrams of shared racks, including device names and positions. Do not post it publicly.
system_settings.rack_embed_regen_confirm: Regenerating invalidates every existing embed URL immediately; each one has to be re-pasted. Continue?
system_settings.rack_embed_regenerated: Token regenerated — existing URLs stopped working
system_settings.cert_expiry_days_hint: The global default. Each certificate can override it on the certificates page — a commercial certificate bought by hand needs lead time, an auto-renewed one does not.
system_settings.liveness_no_aging_warn: Ticking a source marked "never expires" means one sighting keeps the address online forever. Do not tick it unless you know exactly why you want that.
system_settings.backup_enc_hint: The daily backup holds the database and the key that decrypts the secrets in it (backend.env). With a passphrase set, each day's backup is packed and encrypted into one .jtbak file and the plain copy is removed; without one, both sit side by side in plain form.
system_settings.backup_enc_too_short: The passphrase needs at least 12 characters
system_settings.backup_enc_remove_confirm: After removal, later backups are written in plain form again. Continue?
system_settings.backup_enc_keep_hint: Without the passphrase the backups cannot be decrypted: keep it somewhere other than this host (for example a password manager). certOs.win_note: The Windows agent runs on PowerShell 5.1 (built into Windows Server 2019 and later); no extra modules needed. IIS binds a certificate held in the Windows certificate store rather than a file, so the agent imports it, repoints the binding, verifies over a real TLS connection, and rolls back on failure. The HTTPS binding itself must already exist in IIS — the agent swaps the certificate, it does not change site configuration.

certHelpWin.intro: Install one agent on each Windows host that should renew its certificates automatically. The agent periodically asks jt-ipam whether a newer version exists; if so it downloads it, imports it into the Windows certificate store, repoints the IIS HTTPS binding at it, then opens a real TLS connection to confirm the new certificate is being served — and rolls back if it is not.
certHelpWin.step2: Once the agent exists, opening it (from the creation dialog or the list's View button) shows its own install command with the key already filled in. Paste it into an **elevated** PowerShell on the target host.
certHelpWin.step3: After saving the config, do a -DryRun on that host first; once it looks right the scheduled task takes over (advanced: you can also edit the DEPLOY_1_* lines by hand).
certHelpWin.uninstall_label: Remove the agent (from an elevated PowerShell):
certHelpWin.uninstall_note: Removes the scheduled task, the agent, its config and state. **Certificates already imported into the Windows certificate store are left in place** — they are in use by the bindings.
certHelpWin.service_note: Scheduling: a Windows Task Scheduler job named "jt-ipam-cert-agent" (daily by default, running as SYSTEM). Log: C:\ProgramData\jt-ipam-cert-agent\last-run.log. Run once now: schtasks /Run /TN jt-ipam-cert-agent.
certHelpWin.requirements: Requirements: Windows PowerShell 5.1, built into Windows Server 2019 and later (no extra modules, no Python, no OpenSSL). Must run as Administrator — both importing into LocalMachine\My and changing http.sys SSL bindings require it. The IIS HTTPS binding must already exist; the agent swaps the certificate, it does not change site configuration.

netdiag.section_note: These send packets from the jt-ipam server, so results describe reachability from the server to the target, which is not necessarily the same as from your own machine. Target count and concurrency are capped, and each run is written to the audit log.
netdiag.targets_ph: One per line, or comma separated; a CIDR such as 198.51.100.0/28 also works
netdiag.targets_hint: Accepts IPs, hostnames and CIDRs (a network expands to its hosts). Up to {n} targets per run.
netdiag.need_port: Enter at least one valid port
netdiag.trace_hint: Prefers tracepath (no privileges needed, and it reports path MTU — useful for diagnosing MTU black holes). Hops that do not answer are listed rather than omitted.
netdiag.tcp_hint: More reliable than ping for hosts that block ICMP — it tests the service port you actually use.
netdiag.truncated: timed out — showing hops discovered so far
netdiag.udp_note: UDP has no handshake, so silence proves nothing — the port may be open but not replying, filtered by a firewall, or the packet may have been lost. That is reported as its own state rather than as open. "Closed" means an ICMP port unreachable came back. Ports 53 (DNS) and 123 (NTP) get a real protocol packet, so a protocol reply is what makes them definitively open.
netdiag.tls_hint: Shows the certificate the host actually serves. It is fetched without verifying first on purpose — a broken certificate (self-signed, expired, wrong name) is exactly when you need to see it. Whether it validates against the system trust store is reported separately rather than turning into a failure.
netdiag.http_hint: Status, redirect chain and the headers that matter. TLS is not verified by default so you still get a result from a host with certificate problems (use the TLS check above to inspect the certificate).
netdiag.rdns_hint: Looks up PTR records in bulk to find which addresses in a range have no reverse DNS — tedious to establish one lookup at a time.
netdiag.icmp_howto_why: The backend runs as a systemd service whose sandbox (NoNewPrivileges) makes the cap_net_raw file capability on /bin/ping inert — ping works in a shell but cannot send anything from here. It does not mean the target is unreachable. Either option below fixes it.
netdiag.icmp_howto_a: Option A (recommended): widen the kernel's ICMP group range. This permits ICMP echo only — no crafted packets, no sniffing — which is far narrower than granting the whole backend CAP_NET_RAW.
netdiag.icmp_howto_b: Option B: grant CAP_NET_RAW to the backend service. Broader (it allows building arbitrary raw packets); use only if A is not possible.
netdiag.icmp_howto_note: Neither requires reinstalling. A takes effect immediately; B needs a backend restart. The TCP / UDP / TLS / HTTP tools are unaffected — they never needed privileges.
netdiag.ports_hint: Comma- or space-separated. Use “-” for a range, e.g. 8006-8010. Up to 16 ports per run - this is a connectivity check, not a port scanner.
netdiag.port_overflow: Over the limit of {n} ports; only the first ones were checked
netdiag.trace_slow_hint: A hop that does not answer can only be confirmed after its timeout, so 15 hops take roughly 30–60 seconds; rows appear one hop at a time as they arrive, so there is nothing to wait for.
netdiag.not_reached_tip: The last responding hop is not the destination itself. tracepath probes with high UDP ports, which are often filtered late in the path; once traceroute is installed the server switches to ICMP, which almost always gets through.
netdiag.agent_timeout: Timed out waiting for the agent (it may be offline)
netdiag.agent_note: Packets leave from the network where that scan agent runs, not from the jt-ipam host — use it to test reachability inside a customer site. Admins only.

esxi.help_step3: For a self-signed certificate, turn TLS verification off or the connection will be rejected.

autolink.title: Attach IPs to devices by NIC MAC
autolink.enable_hint: Each sync round (about 5 minutes), attach addresses that have no device but whose MAC matches a device's physical port. Off by default.
autolink.scope_hint: With overlapping subnets, you can restrict this to the ranges you know are clean.
autolink.rules_hint: Only fills what is empty; never overwrites and never removes an existing link. A MAC found on several devices, a protocol-reserved or non-unicast MAC, a hostname naming a different device, a customer conflict, an archived subnet — all are skipped rather than guessed. Every change is written to the IP change log, so it can be traced and undone.

sftp.rename_no_slash: Names cannot contain / — rename only works within the same directory.
sftp.delete_confirm: Delete {name}? This runs on the remote host and cannot be undone.
sftp.truncated: This directory has a very large number of entries, so only the first part was fetched — page through what was fetched below; for the rest, open a subdirectory or use the terminal.
sftp.connect_hint: SFTP: browse and transfer files on this host
sftp.enable_hint: When enabled, authorized users can open the SFTP file browser from this IP's detail page. Independent of SSH: file transfer can be allowed without a terminal (same permission strength, over the same SSH connection).
sftp.err_ws_closed: The connection closed before it was established (code {code}). On a freshly upgraded site, or behind your own reverse proxy, this usually means the proxy is not forwarding the WebSocket upgrade headers — check that the console location in nginx lists sftp.
sftp.filter_note: Showing {shown} of {total} entries in this directory.
sftp.batch_delete_confirm: Delete the {n} selected entries? This runs on the remote host and cannot be undone.
sftp.batch_no_files: No files in the selection — directories cannot be downloaded directly.
sftp.batch_downloaded_skipped_dirs: Downloaded {n} file(s); skipped {dirs} director(ies), which cannot be downloaded directly
sftp.drop_dirs_skipped: {n} folders could not be expanded and were skipped (this browser does not expose folder contents)
sftp.move_path_ph: Type an absolute destination path, or pick one below
sftp.move_no_subdirs: No subdirectories here (you can still move into this directory, or type a path above)
sftp.delete_dir_warning: This deletes everything inside it and cannot be undone. Symbolic links are removed as links; whatever they point to is left alone.
sftp.batch_dirs_not_empty: These folders are not empty and were left alone: {names}. Delete them one at a time to choose whether to remove their contents.
sftp.offline_hint: This listing is what was on screen before the connection dropped and may no longer match the remote host. Reconnect to work with files again.
sftp.sort_mode_hint: With Folders first, directories always come before files in both ascending and descending order, like a file manager. Mixed sorts purely by the selected column, like ls. The choice is saved to your preferences and follows you to other devices.
sftp.unreadable_item: This item cannot be read (compress a folder into a single file first)
sftp.offline_code: Close code {code} (1000 = closed normally; 1006 = the connection was cut mid-way, usually an idle timeout in an intervening reverse proxy)
sftp.offline_upload: An upload was in flight when the connection dropped: {name} — {sent} of {total} sent
sftp.drop_too_many: {n} items were left out (at most {max} files per drop)
sftp.err_no_ack: The data is not reaching the server: 15 seconds after the first block was sent, none of it had been acknowledged. The server is fine (it already replied that it is ready to receive) — something between this computer and the server is dropping the data, commonly a VPN or proxy discarding larger packets, or a browser extension interfering. Try an incognito window (extensions off) or a different network.
sftp.err_big_needs_fs_api: This browser cannot write straight to disk; a file over {max} would have to be held in memory and would crash the tab. Use Chrome or Edge, or scp / WinSCP.
sftp.conflict_title: A file with this name already exists
sftp.conflict_safe: The upload replaces it only once it is complete; if it fails or is cancelled, the existing file is left as it was.
sftp.conflict_apply_all: Do the same for the other files that already exist

fw_autocreate.label: Create addresses IPAM does not have
fw_autocreate.hint: While syncing DHCP leases, create a record for an address IPAM does not know yet (only inside this firewall's associated subnets, and only when the subnet is unambiguous). When off, such data is skipped and the sync summary reports how many were skipped.
fw_autocreate.risk: Risk: a machine that obtained a DHCP address is not necessarily a machine that belongs in IPAM. Someone plugging in an unauthorised device and getting a lease would be recorded as a legitimate entry — and once it is in IPAM it no longer appears under "unauthorised IPs" in anomaly detection, whose whole test is "seen in ARP, absent from IPAM". Auto-created records are flagged as unregistered in the IP list; review them regularly.

virt_autocreate.label: Trust addresses reported by virtualization (create ones IPAM lacks)
virt_autocreate.hint: During sync, create a record when a VM or node address is not yet in IPAM (only within the configured subnet scope, and only when the subnet is unambiguous). When off, only existing records are matched.
virt_autocreate.risk: Risk: an address visible on the hypervisor is not necessarily one that belongs in IPAM (test machines, throwaway clones, systems someone else manages). And once recorded, that address stops appearing under "unauthorised IPs" in anomaly detection, whose whole test is "seen in ARP, absent from IPAM". Auto-created records are flagged as unregistered in the IP list; review them regularly.

scan_agents.auto_create_ips_hint: When a scan finds an address that IPAM does not have, create a record for it (marked as discovered by the scan agent, with a purple marker in the list and the grid). Off by default: once an address is recorded, unauthorised-IP detection no longer lists it, so a machine someone plugged in without asking would quietly become an official record. While this is off, no record is created and the sighting is remembered instead: the grid shows the address as "Unmanaged" and unauthorised-IP detection lists it.

fw_changes.title: Firewall rule changes
fw_changes.baseline: (first snapshot, used as the comparison baseline)
fw_changes.hint: Every sync round compares each firewall's rules (OPNsense / pfSense / FortiGate / Palo Alto / Check Point / MikroTik); only a real change is recorded and notified. A permit rule that appears overnight is a classic sign of a breach or a backdoor — this page is the record you check it against.
fw_changes.ai_done: AI analysis finished — click View result

surface.title: Exposed services list
surface.empty_fqdn: No exposed service resolves from a known FQDN
surface.no_fqdn_note: Another {n} exposed service(s) have no DNS name and appear only under "By IP".
surface.hint: An inventory of externally reachable IPs and ports, each with its IPAM identity. “Unregistered” means an external opening points at a host IPAM does not know — a red flag in itself.
surface.scope_note: Only unambiguous openings are listed (NAT forwards and WAN passes targeting a single IP); rules targeting aliases / any / networks are not expanded; FortiGate sources join once verified per vendor.
surface.empty: No determinable external openings (or no firewall integrated yet).
surface.paired_tip: The same target IP and port has both a NAT forward and a permit rule — they belong together (port forwards usually carry an associated rule).

zabbix.title: Zabbix integration
zabbix.intro: Zabbix complements the monitoring picture: host-to-IP mapping, availability, maintenance windows, and a monitoring coverage gap (addresses IPAM knows about but Zabbix does not monitor). Read-only — nothing in Zabbix is modified. ARP/FDB are not part of Zabbix's built-in data; keep using LibreNMS for those.
zabbix.url_hint: The Zabbix frontend URL is enough (/api_jsonrpc.php is appended automatically). API tokens require Zabbix 5.4 or newer.
zabbix.gap_scoped: Within the configured subnet scope, {n} address(es) with a known hostname are not monitored by this Zabbix.
zabbix.gap_global: {n} address(es) with a known hostname are not monitored by this Zabbix (no subnet scope configured on this instance).

event_rules.title: Event rules
event_rules.intro: Event → conditions → actions. For example: notify only when a new subnet's description contains Production, or alert on an unauthorised IP only inside server ranges. Conditions are structured fields, not an executable expression, and regular expressions are deliberately not supported — rules are user input, and anything executable is a risk.
event_rules.events_ph: type your own; * matches every event
event_rules.conditions_hint: Fields use dot paths, e.g. data.subnet.cidr, data.count. No conditions means the event name alone decides.
event_rules.notify_title_ph: Notification title (defaults to the rule name)
event_rules.test_hint: Only evaluates whether it would match — no notification or webhook is sent.
event_rules.would_match: This payload would match the rule
event_rules.bad_json: The payload is not valid JSON

paloalto.title: Palo Alto
paloalto.intro: Read-only sync from Palo Alto via the PAN-OS API (reads only — nothing on the firewall is changed). Needs an API key for a read-only role, and the backend must be able to reach the management interface.
paloalto.key_hint: Create a read-only administrator in PAN-OS, then obtain an API key via /api/?type=keygen. The key is sent in the X-PAN-KEY header.
paloalto.api_version_hint: Leave blank to auto-detect (recommended). PAN-OS REST URLs carry a version segment (/restapi/v11.1/…); a wrong value makes every endpoint return 404.
paloalto.vsys_ph: Blank = discover every vsys (or list them: vsys1, vsys2)
paloalto.none_configured: No Palo Alto firewall configured — add one under Admin → Palo Alto integration.

checkpoint.title: Check Point
checkpoint.intro: Read-only sync of gateways, network objects, access rules and NAT through the Management API of a Check Point management server (Security Management Server / Multi-Domain). The login asks for a read-only session and nothing is ever changed. All gateways and policy packages managed by the server appear here; the IP detail firewall lookup, rule change detection and IP change assessment use them. The gateways' DHCP settings, ARP table and DHCP leases are in the Gateways tab, where each gateway gets its own Gaia connection. Verified on a real R81.20 system; still marked Beta.
checkpoint.api_url_hint: HTTPS address of the management server (same as the Gaia web portal), e.g. https://mgmt.example.test; do not add /web_api. For Smart-1 Cloud use the API URL it gives you.
checkpoint.secret_keep: API key / password (leave empty to keep)
checkpoint.secret_required: Enter the API key or password
checkpoint.username_required: Password login needs a user name
checkpoint.domains_hint: Leave empty for a single management server; for Multi-Domain list the domains to sync (one login per domain).
checkpoint.packages_hint: Empty = all policy packages; list names (e.g. Standard) to limit the sync.
checkpoint.setup_hint: Create a dedicated administrator in SmartConsole: permission profile Read Only All, authentication API Key, then paste the key here. Under Manage & Settings → Blades → Management API → Advanced Settings allow connections from the jt-ipam host (All IP addresses that can be used for GUI clients, or a specific address) and run api restart.
checkpoint.test_line: {domain}: API {version}. Gateways {gateways}. Hosts {hosts}. Networks {networks}. Policy packages {packages}
checkpoint.test_partial: Some items could not be read: {detail}
checkpoint.search: Search name, source, destination, service, comments
checkpoint.rules_hint: Access rules saved by the last sync, ordered by domain / policy package / layer / rule number (Check Point matches top-down). Inline-layer rules show as "parent › inline layer"; a field tagged "except" means "anything except these".
checkpoint.objects_hint: Network objects saved by the last sync: hosts, networks, address ranges, groups and groups with exclusion. The IP detail firewall lookup matches against this list.
checkpoint.gateways_hint: Gateways and servers registered on the management server (their addresses are added to the rogue-DHCP allowlist). Each gateway can get its own Gaia API connection to read its DHCP settings, ARP table and leases; anything the account may not read is skipped automatically.
checkpoint.gaia_delete_confirm: Remove the Gaia connection of this gateway? The pools, lease flags and host names it synced are taken back too.
checkpoint.gaia_url_hint: Same address as the gateway's Gaia portal, followed by /gaia_api, e.g. https://<gateway>/gaia_api.
checkpoint.gaia_tls_hint: Gaia uses a self-signed certificate by default; turn verification off unless it was replaced (traffic stays HTTPS-encrypted).
checkpoint.gaia_sync_dhcp: DHCP server settings (read only): pools, default gateway and DNS handed to clients
checkpoint.gaia_allow_scripts: Read the ARP table and DHCP leases (runs fixed read commands on the gateway)
checkpoint.gaia_scripts_warning: The Gaia API has no command that reads the ARP table or leases, so jt-ipam uses run-script to run two fixed read commands on the gateway (ip -s neigh show, reading /var/lib/dhcpd/dhcpd.leases); nothing is changed. This needs an account that may run commands; with a read-only account these two are skipped automatically, the DHCP settings still sync and the sync does not count as failed.
checkpoint.gaia_setup_hint: Connects to the gateway's own Gaia API (a different account from the management server's API key). A read-only Gaia role can read the DHCP settings; the ARP table and leases need an account that may run commands and are skipped otherwise.
checkpoint.gaia_test_ok: Connected: Gaia API {version}. DHCP subnets {subnets}. Read commands: {scripts}
checkpoint.gaia_scripts_denied: account lacks permission (ARP and leases will be skipped)
checkpoint.gaia_dhcp_hint: The gateway's DHCP server settings from the last sync. Pools have exclusions removed and disabled ranges skipped; the default gateway and DNS are used by IP change assessment. When the gateway's DHCP server is turned off as a whole, every subnet shows as disabled (the settings remain, but nothing is handed out).
checkpoint.gaia_scripts_unsupported: not supported by this Gaia (ARP and leases will be skipped)
checkpoint.gaia_skip_no_permission: the account may not run commands
checkpoint.gaia_skip_unsupported: this Gaia API has no run-script
checkpoint.gaia_skip_no_lease_file: no lease file on the gateway
checkpoint.gaia_skip_dhcp_off: the DHCP server is not enabled
checkpoint.gaia_where_hint: Gateway DHCP settings, the ARP table and DHCP leases are not set here: they live on the gateway itself (Gaia), so set up a Gaia connection for each gateway in the Gateways tab (with the gateway's account, not this API key).
checkpoint.gaia_where_after_save: After saving and syncing once, the gateways appear in the Gateways tab.

mikrotik.title: MikroTik RouterOS
mikrotik.intro: Read-only pull over the RouterOS v7 REST API (the www-ssl service must be enabled and the account needs api + read). This integration never changes anything on the device. RouterOS 6.x has no REST API and is not supported.
mikrotik.diag_absent: this device does not have that feature
mikrotik.diag_hint: Row counts and timings are how you decide whether to enable a section: turn off the expensive ones, or lengthen the sync interval.
mikrotik.url_hint: The RouterOS management address (HTTPS). /rest is appended automatically.
mikrotik.pw_hint: Create a read-only group account on RouterOS (api + read only) rather than using admin.
mikrotik.heavy_hint: ARP and FDB read the whole table, which can be tens of thousands of rows on a large router, so they are off by default — run Test connection first and look at the row count and timing.
mikrotik.guard_intro: A MikroTik is often the site's main router. Syncing always runs sequentially, pauses between sections, and stops the rest of the round once CPU load passes the threshold. That keeps the impact low, but any query costs the router some CPU — there is no zero-impact option.
mikrotik.cpu_limit_hint: CPU load is re-read after each section; above the threshold the remaining sections are skipped until the next round.
mikrotik.section_delay_hint: Back-to-back requests keep the router's API service pegged on one core; a short pause makes a real difference.
mikrotik.max_response_hint: The RouterOS REST API has no pagination, so this is the only guardrail; the section aborts and reports when exceeded.
mikrotik.interval_hint: Defaults to 900s (other integrations use 300). For a main router, 1800 is reasonable.
mikrotik.device_auto: Auto: the device that owns the API address
mikrotik.device_hint: Interfaces, FDB and neighbors are stored on a device. Leave empty to use the device that owns the IP of the API address; if none matches, these three sections are skipped (not a failure)
mikrotik.neighbors_hint: Neighbors the router heard via LLDP/CDP/MNDP. A neighbor links to its device when its announced address or MAC matches exactly one

jump_hosts.title: Jump hosts
jump_hosts.fp_mismatch: Fingerprint does NOT match the pinned one. This may be a man-in-the-middle — do not trust it until you know why.
jump_hosts.fp_unpinned: No host key pinned yet. Check the fingerprint above with whoever runs the jump host, then press Trust and save.
jump_hosts.max_sessions_hint: Console sessions share one SSH connection, but each forward still costs the jump host resources.
jump_hosts.pin_required: A jump host sits in the middle of the whole connection: after saving, press Test connection, check the host key fingerprint and pin it. Consoles will not route through it until then.
jump_hosts.delete_in_use: {subnets} subnet(s) and {ips} address(es) currently point at this jump host. Deleting it sends them back to a direct connection — with overlapping ranges that can mean reaching a different customer. Delete anyway?
jump_hosts.intro: Consoles (SSH / SFTP / RDP / VNC) can go "server → jump host → target" when the server cannot reach a site directly but can reach an SSH host there (for example over a VPN back to headquarters). If the site already has a scan agent, use relay through the scan agent instead; no jump host is needed. The exit is set on the subnet and can be overridden per IP. BMC uses UDP and cannot go through a jump host.
jump_hosts.exit_hint: How consoles reach this. Blank = direct (on an address, blank means it follows the subnet).
jump_hosts.help_link: What does a jump host need?
jump_hosts.help_when: A jump host is an SSH host that the server can reach and that can reach the targets; nothing from jt-ipam is installed on it. If the site already has a scan agent, relay through the agent instead; a jump host suits sites where an agent cannot be installed but an SSH host is available.
jump_hosts.req_os: Any host running an SSH server that allows TCP forwarding: OpenSSH on Linux or BSD is the usual choice; the OpenSSH Server built into Windows and network devices that support SSH forwarding work too. Older SSH algorithms are supported.
jump_hosts.req_net: The jt-ipam server must reach the jump host's SSH port, and the jump host must reach the targets' console ports (SSH 22, RDP 3389, VNC from 5900, or whatever you use).
jump_hosts.req_fwd: The SSH server must allow local forwarding (OpenSSH allows it by default). Change AllowTcpForwarding no or DisableForwarding yes; if PermitOpen is used it must include the targets and ports.
jump_hosts.req_account: No root and no shell needed: jt-ipam only logs in and forwards, it never runs a command on the jump host. A dedicated forwarding-only account is recommended (example below).
jump_hosts.req_auth: Key (recommended) or password. Paste the private key in OpenSSH or PEM format (Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA); passphrase-protected keys are not supported.
jump_hosts.req_hostkey: After saving, click Test connection, check the fingerprint with the jump host's administrator and then click Trust and save. Consoles do not use the jump host until it is pinned, and refuse if the fingerprint later changes (possible interception).
jump_hosts.help_setup_title: Example: a forwarding-only account on Linux (OpenSSH)
jump_hosts.help_setup_note: This account gets no shell and no terminal; it can only forward. Paste the private key into the Private key (PEM) field and use jtipam-jump as the username.
jump_hosts.help_limits: The BMC console uses UDP and cannot go through a jump host. Console sessions share one SSH connection, and each jump host has a session limit. A disabled jump host refuses instead of connecting directly (so overlapping networks never reach the wrong host).
jump_hosts.tab: SSH jump hosts (sites without an agent)

ocs.title: OCS Inventory integration
ocs.intro: Pull endpoint and server asset inventory (hostname, OS, NICs, serial/model) from OCS Inventory. Read-only; never changes OCS. Matches existing IPs by MAC only — it never creates IPs on its own.
ocs.auth_optional: Optional (OCS REST has no auth by default)
ocs.password_kept: Leave blank to keep the stored password
ocs.sync_software_hint: Off by default: inflates each host from ~2 KB to ~80 KB (software is not yet stored in this version).
ocs.agents_hint: One row per OCS computer: a computer with several IPs is listed once.
ocs.warn_unauthenticated: ⚠️ This OCS returns data with no credentials — anyone who can reach it can read the whole asset inventory. Add authentication for /ocsapi on the OCS side (Apache), or restrict access with a reverse proxy.
ocs.scope_hint: Only match MACs of IPs within these subnets; “IPs without an agent” also lists only these subnets. Empty = global.

ranges.auto_hint: Created from the DHCP range detected on {source} and kept in sync with it; change it on the DHCP server instead
ranges.auto_desc: Created from the detected DHCP range
ranges.title: Address ranges (pools)
ranges.hint: A run of consecutive addresses inside {cidr}, such as a DHCP pool or addresses kept for certain devices. Ranges used as a DHCP pool also mark their addresses as "in a DHCP range". DHCP ranges detected by integrations are added automatically.
ranges.assign_hint: Add an IP record with this address
ranges.delete_confirm: Delete range {range}? IP records inside it are kept.

scan_load.title: Scan load: {name}
scan_load.no_data: This agent has not reported cycle statistics yet (agent 1.10.0 and later; they appear on the next cycle after it updates).
scan_load.backlog_line: Background queue (name lookups, OS fingerprint): {n} hosts
scan_load.trend: Duration of the last {n} cycles (dashed line is the interval)
scan_load.no_suggestions: The load is normal; nothing to change.
scan_load.move_confirm: Have the selected agent scan {cidr}? That agent must be on the same network segment to see MACs and NetBIOS names.
scan_load.sg_move_subnets: A liveness cycle takes longer than the interval. Moving {subnets} to another agent brings it under {target}%.
scan_load.sg_raise_interval: A liveness cycle takes longer than the interval ({interval} s). Raise the interval to at least {suggested} s, or add an agent to share the load.
scan_load.sg_slow_subnet: {cidr} takes {per_host_ms} ms per address, much slower than the other subnets ({median_ms} ms) — usually a WAN link or a firewall. Consider an agent at that site.
scan_load.sg_split_large: {cidr} has {total} addresses but the agent scans only the first {scanned} each cycle; the rest are never scanned. Split it into smaller subnets in IPAM, or spread it over several agents.

scan_load.sg_rotating_large: {cidr} has {total} addresses and takes {rounds} cycles (about {minutes} min) to cover once. The online threshold is {threshold} min; if covering takes longer, hosts show offline between scans — split it into smaller subnets in IPAM, or spread it over several agents.

kea_dhcp.title: Kea DHCP Server
kea_dhcp.intro: Connects to Kea's JSON control API and syncs pools, reservations and leases read-only; nothing on Kea is changed. For Kea 2.x enter the Control Agent (kea-ctrl-agent) URL; from Kea 3.0 the DHCP server's own HTTP control socket also works, and the two are told apart automatically. For Kea running on OPNsense or pfSense use that firewall's integration instead.
kea_dhcp.api_url_hint: For example http://kea.example.test:8000/. If Kea is on a private network the backend needs OUTBOUND_ALLOW_PRIVATE.
